stem: A compliance reviewer asks where customer data is actually processed when a scheduled job runs in a Databricks workspace that uses classic compute rather than serverless. The reviewer needs to name the cloud account that holds those processing resources, and has already confirmed that the workspace web application is not in scope for this control.

option_texts.A: In the classic compute plane, which runs inside the customer's own cloud account
option_texts.B: In the control plane, which Databricks manages outside the classic compute plane
option_texts.C: In the serverless compute plane, which Databricks runs in its own cloud account
option_texts.D: In the Unity Catalog metastore, which governs the customer tables the job reads

drill_answer_short: Classic compute resources run in the customer's own cloud account, in the classic compute plane
decision_hinge: For classic Databricks compute, the compute resources are in your cloud account in what is called the classic compute plane; the control plane is located in the Databricks account.

plausible_options.C: needs to name the cloud account that holds those processing resources

eliminated_by.B: the workspace web application is not in scope for this control

D.signal: where customer data is actually processed
D.requires_fact: Unity Catalog metastores are the central governance system for data assets such as tables and models; the compute plane is where data is processed.

distractor_traps.B: T2: wrong layer — the control plane holds backend services and the web application, which the stem puts out of scope, not the processing resources
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — serverless compute is also a compute plane that processes data, but it runs in the Databricks account rather than the customer's
distractor_traps.D: T2: wrong layer — a metastore governs data assets rather than executing the workload

stem: An engineer inspecting a Delta table's directory on cloud storage finds a _delta_log folder sitting alongside the table's data files. An auditor wants to know which format the commit history itself is written in, separate from the format holding the table rows.

option_texts.A: Data files in JSON and the transaction log in Parquet
option_texts.B: Data files in Parquet and the transaction log in JSON
option_texts.C: Data files in Parquet and the transaction log also in Parquet
option_texts.D: Data files in Parquet and the transaction log in XML

drill_answer_short: Delta stores rows as Parquet data files and the commit history as JSON in _delta_log
decision_hinge: Delta Lake builds on standard formats: table data is stored in Parquet data files, and the transaction log is written as JSON.

plausible_options.A: separate from the format holding the table rows

eliminated_by.C: which format the commit history itself is written in

D.signal: finds a _delta_log folder sitting alongside the table's data files
D.requires_fact: Delta Lake extends Parquet data files with a file-based transaction log for ACID transactions and scalable metadata handling.

distractor_traps.A: T3: confusable sibling — the two real formats are named, but swapped between the data files and the log
distractor_traps.C: T4: breaks a stated requirement — the auditor asked for the log format separate from the row format, and this names one format for both
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — Delta Lake does not write any part of a table in XML

stem: A security questionnaire asks a platform team to state where notebook source files and SQL queries are persisted for a classic Databricks workspace. The team must distinguish those workspace assets from the backend services Databricks runs, and the assets must remain available after every cluster has terminated.

option_texts.A: In the control plane, next to the backend services that run the workspace web application
option_texts.B: In the Unity Catalog metastore, next to the governed tables and volumes it already tracks
option_texts.C: In workspace storage, which for classic workspaces sits in the customer's cloud account
option_texts.D: In the cluster file system of the classic compute resource that last opened them

drill_answer_short: Notebooks and SQL queries are workspace file system data, held in workspace storage
decision_hinge: The workspace file system stores assets users create through the UI — notebooks, SQL queries and dashboards, alerts, and libraries — in workspace storage, and for a classic workspace that storage bucket is in the customer's cloud account.

plausible_options.A: distinguish those workspace assets from the backend services Databricks runs

B.signal: where notebook source files and SQL queries are persisted
B.requires_fact: Workspace file system data is separate from a customer's own data objects such as Unity Catalog tables and volumes.

eliminated_by.D: the assets must remain available after every cluster has terminated

distractor_traps.A: T3: confusable sibling — the control plane really does host the backend services and the web application, but not the workspace file assets themselves
distractor_traps.B: T2: wrong layer — Unity Catalog governs data objects, not the notebooks and queries users author
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated requirement — cluster storage disappears when the compute resource terminates

stem: A platform architect is documenting how data assets are addressed after several regional workspaces were attached to one metastore. Two teams currently use the same table name in different projects, so the documented addressing scheme has to keep those two tables distinct without renaming either one.

option_texts.A: A two-level schema and table name, scoped to each attached workspace separately
option_texts.B: A four-level namespace of metastore, catalog, schema, and object per workspace
option_texts.C: A storage path under the workspace bucket that each attached workspace resolves
option_texts.D: A three-level namespace of catalog, schema, and object managed by Unity Catalog

drill_answer_short: Unity Catalog addresses data through a three-level catalog.schema.object namespace
decision_hinge: In a Unity Catalog metastore you organize data under a three-level namespace of catalog name, schema name, and object name.

plausible_options.B: keep those two tables distinct without renaming either one

A.signal: Two teams currently use the same table name in different projects
A.requires_fact: Data and AI assets such as tables, views, volumes, functions, and models follow a three-level namespace in Unity Catalog.

eliminated_by.C: several regional workspaces were attached to one metastore

distractor_traps.A: T6: stale behaviour — the two-level namespace is the legacy Hive metastore model that Unity Catalog replaced
distractor_traps.B: T8: scope error — the metastore is the container that holds catalogs, not a fourth part of an object's name
distractor_traps.C: T2: wrong layer — Unity Catalog addresses governed objects by name rather than by storage path

stem: An engineer must produce an audit trail for a governed Delta table showing every operation applied over the past month, including when each change committed and which principal issued it. A snapshot of the rows as they looked last Tuesday would not satisfy the auditor, who wants the operations themselves.

option_texts.A: DESCRIBE HISTORY on the table, which lists each operation with its timestamp
option_texts.B: DESCRIBE DETAIL on the table, which reports its current state on storage
option_texts.C: DESCRIBE EXTENDED on the table, which reports schema rather than operation history
option_texts.D: SELECT with VERSION AS OF, which reads the table at an earlier version

drill_answer_short: DESCRIBE HISTORY returns the operation log — timestamp, operation, and user per commit
decision_hinge: DESCRIBE HISTORY returns an ordered list of a Delta table's operations with the timestamp, operation type, and the user or principal that ran each one.

plausible_options.B: showing every operation applied over the past month

C.signal: including when each change committed and which principal issued it
C.requires_fact: DESCRIBE EXTENDED returns a table's schema and extended metadata, not a list of commits.

eliminated_by.D: A snapshot of the rows as they looked last Tuesday would not satisfy the auditor

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — DESCRIBE DETAIL describes the table as it stands now rather than the sequence of commits that produced it
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — another DESCRIBE variant, but one that reports structure instead of operations
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated requirement — time travel returns row snapshots, which the stem rules out

stem: A team is deciding how much custom tooling it still needs after standardising on Delta tables in Unity Catalog. They want to know which guarantees come from the table format itself, so they can delete the home-grown scripts that currently duplicate them. Select TWO capabilities Delta Lake provides natively.

option_texts.A: Rejecting a write whose columns do not conform to the target table schema
option_texts.B: Adding new optional columns to a table without rewriting it by hand
option_texts.C: Removing every superseded version automatically at the end of each write
option_texts.D: Replacing the underlying cloud object storage the table files live on
option_texts.E: Encrypting each column with a separate customer-supplied key on write

drill_answer_short: Schema enforcement rejects non-conforming writes; schema evolution adds new columns
decision_hinge: Delta Lake provides schema enforcement, which rejects writes that do not match the table schema, and schema evolution, which lets new columns be added without recreating the table.

plausible_options.C: delete the home-grown scripts that currently duplicate them

D.signal: which guarantees come from the table format itself
D.requires_fact: Delta Lake is the optimized storage layer that provides the foundation for tables in a lakehouse on Databricks.

eliminated_by.E: standardising on Delta tables in Unity Catalog

distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — Delta does retain superseded versions to support time travel, and only removes files when VACUUM is run
distractor_traps.D: T2: wrong layer — object storage is the substrate Delta writes onto, not something it supplies
distractor_traps.E: T1: fabricated — per-column customer-key encryption is not a native Delta table capability

stem: Twenty analysts run unpredictable ad hoc SQL against curated Delta tables throughout the working day. The team wants queries to start without waiting for infrastructure to spin up, wants concurrent users isolated from each other, and wants to stop paying for capacity during the quiet hours between bursts.

option_texts.A: An all-purpose compute resource with a fixed number of worker nodes attached
option_texts.B: A serverless SQL warehouse, which starts instantly and scales with demand
option_texts.C: A job compute resource sized for the heaviest scheduled overnight workload
option_texts.D: A single-node compute resource shared by all of the analysts at once

drill_answer_short: Serverless SQL warehouses give instant startup and elastic scaling for concurrent SQL
decision_hinge: A serverless SQL warehouse provides instant and elastic compute that eliminates waiting for infrastructure and avoids over-provisioning during usage spikes, with intelligent workload management handling scaling.

plausible_options.A: wants concurrent users isolated from each other

eliminated_by.C: unpredictable ad hoc SQL against curated Delta tables throughout the working day
eliminated_by.D: stop paying for capacity during the quiet hours between bursts

distractor_traps.A: T3: confusable sibling — all-purpose compute does serve interactive users, but a fixed worker count cannot release capacity between bursts
distractor_traps.C: T2: wrong layer — job compute exists to run scheduled workloads, not interactive analyst queries
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated requirement — one shared node cannot isolate twenty concurrent users

stem: An architect is designing a hybrid platform whose SQL layer must reach databases that stay inside the enterprise's own custom-defined network, including systems hosted on-premises. Compliance will not allow the query compute layer to sit outside that network, and the team still wants Photon and Predictive IO.

option_texts.A: A serverless SQL warehouse, whose compute layer Databricks runs for the customer
option_texts.B: A classic SQL warehouse, which omits Predictive IO and gives entry-level speed
option_texts.C: A pro SQL warehouse, whose compute layer stays inside the customer's own account
option_texts.D: A serverless job compute resource, which Databricks provisions inside its account

drill_answer_short: Pro SQL warehouses keep compute in the customer account, for custom networks and on-prem federation
decision_hinge: Use a pro SQL warehouse when you have custom-defined networking and want to connect to databases in your network in the cloud or on-premises for federation or a hybrid architecture; its compute layer exists in your own account rather than the Databricks account.

plausible_options.A: the team still wants Photon and Predictive IO

eliminated_by.B: the team still wants Photon and Predictive IO

D.signal: designing a hybrid platform whose SQL layer must reach databases
D.requires_fact: Serverless compute resources run in a serverless compute plane inside the Databricks account rather than inside the customer's custom-defined network.

distractor_traps.A: T3: confusable sibling — serverless warehouses support both performance features, but run their compute layer outside the customer's network
distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — a classic warehouse does keep compute in the customer account, but it does not support Predictive IO
distractor_traps.D: T2: wrong layer — job compute runs scheduled workloads rather than serving the SQL layer

stem: A nightly ETL pipeline currently runs on an all-purpose compute resource whose auto-termination is set to six hours. The pipeline finishes somewhere between one and three hours depending on volume, and the team wants to cut spend without changing when the pipeline is triggered or how large it can scale.

option_texts.A: Shorten the auto-termination window on the existing all-purpose compute resource
option_texts.B: Leave the resource running continuously so that startup time is never paid again
option_texts.C: Replace the worker nodes with smaller instance types for the nightly pipeline
option_texts.D: Move the pipeline onto job compute, which terminates when the run ends

drill_answer_short: Job compute is billed at a lower rate and is torn down the moment the run finishes
decision_hinge: Databricks does not recommend configuring tasks with classic all-purpose compute for production jobs; classic jobs compute is configured with the same settings as all-purpose compute.

plausible_options.A: the team wants to cut spend without changing when the pipeline is triggered

eliminated_by.B: finishes somewhere between one and three hours depending on volume
eliminated_by.C: or how large it can scale

distractor_traps.A: T8: scope error — a shorter window trims idle time but still pays the all-purpose rate and still idles after every run
distractor_traps.B: T5: right diagnosis, wrong symptom — startup time is not what is costing the team money here
distractor_traps.C: T4: breaks a stated requirement — smaller workers cap how large the pipeline can scale

stem: A platform team wants to adopt spot instances to lower compute spend, but only where an unexpected reclaim by the cloud provider would not breach a commitment. They need to nominate one workload to start with, knowing that any interrupted run has to be safe to simply start again.

option_texts.A: An overnight batch transformation that is idempotent and configured to retry
option_texts.B: A streaming pipeline carrying a contractual end-to-end latency commitment
option_texts.C: An interactive session where analysts explore data together during the day
option_texts.D: A transactional serving workload fielding many concurrent user requests

drill_answer_short: Spot fits fault-tolerant, retryable batch work where an interruption costs only a rerun
decision_hinge: Configure spot instances for workloads that have lax latency requirements to optimize costs.

plausible_options.C: wants to adopt spot instances to lower compute spend

eliminated_by.B: where an unexpected reclaim by the cloud provider would not breach a commitment
eliminated_by.D: any interrupted run has to be safe to simply start again

distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated requirement — a latency commitment is exactly the kind of promise a reclaim would breach
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — interactive sessions do tolerate restarts technically, but losing a session mid-exploration disrupts the analysts rather than retrying cleanly
distractor_traps.D: T2: wrong layer — a serving workload needs continuous availability rather than cheap interruptible capacity
